name: Lenore Tawney
bio: Lenore Tawney (1907–2007) helped turn weaving into sculpture. She studied sculpture with Alexander Archipenko and tapestry with the Finnish weaver Martta Taipale, and in 1957 moved from Chicago to a loft at Coenties Slip in lower Manhattan, where her neighbours included Agnes Martin, Ellsworth Kelly and Robert Indiana. There she developed open-warp weaving, leaving areas of bare warp so light and air pass through the cloth, and built tall, narrow, freestanding 'woven forms' in linen that hang like columns or figures. Dark River (1962) is over four metres tall. From the late 1970s she made 'Clouds', installations of thousands of linen threads hanging from a ceiling grid, and in parallel produced collages, assemblages, drawings on graph paper and artist's books full of feathers, eggs, bones and text.
studyNotes: Weave space, not just cloth. Open warps let light and the wall show through; what is left unwoven matters as much as the woven parts.
Vertical scale. The woven forms are much taller than a person and hang free of the wall, so they read as sculpture.
Thread as line and volume. In the Cloud works, thousands of single threads make a volume you can walk under; each thread is a drawn line.
Small and large practices feed each other. The intimate collages and books sit alongside monumental weavings; compare their materials and rhythms.
